today.statusLate: Running a little late. That happens.

phaseDescription.menstrual: Hormones are at their lowest, so cramps and tiredness are common. Keep your belly warm and rest a little more.
phaseDescription.follicular: Estrogen is rising and energy usually follows — a good stretch for exercise or getting things done.
phaseDescription.ovulation: LH surges to release an egg, so you might feel a brief twinge on one side — this is also your most fertile day.
phaseDescription.luteal: Progesterone is rising, which can bring tender breasts or a shorter temper. Be gentle with yourself.

learn.title: Understanding your cycle
learn.intro: The menstrual cycle is the body's repeating monthly process that prepares for a possible pregnancy. A cycle runs from the first day of bleeding to the first day of the next period.

howCounted.title: How long is normal?
howCounted.body: Most cycles last 24 to 38 days, averaging around 28.

phase.menstrual: The egg from last cycle wasn't fertilized, so the uterine lining breaks down and sheds — this is your period, usually lasting 3 to 7 days.
phase.follicular: Starting alongside your period, the pituitary gland prompts your ovaries to grow follicles while rising estrogen thickens the uterine lining again.
phase.ovulation: Around the middle of the cycle (day 14 in a 28-day cycle), a surge of LH causes a mature follicle to burst and release an egg.
phase.luteal: After ovulation, the burst follicle becomes the corpus luteum and releases progesterone to keep the lining thick. Without fertilization, it breaks down, hormones drop, and the next period begins.

doctor.title: When to see a doctor
doctor.intro: Check in with a doctor if you notice:
doctor.item1: A cycle shorter than 24 days or longer than 38 days
doctor.item2: No period for 3 months or more
doctor.item3: Bleeding that lasts more than 8 days, or unusually heavy flow
doctor.item4: Severe pain with nausea during your period

formula.sentence: We look at your recent cycles, weigh the newest ones more, and use that to predict your next one.

learnMore.title: Learn more
learnMore.lutealPhase: We assume a 14-day luteal phase unless your temperature readings tell us otherwise.
learnMore.fertileWindowStart: The fertile window starts 5 days before estimated ovulation because sperm can live that long.
learnMore.limits: Calendar-based estimates are a guide, not a guarantee.

legend.title: What the letters mean
legend.cycleLength: C = length of one past cycle, in days
legend.periodStart: P = the date a period started
legend.weight: w = how much a cycle counts; newer cycles count more
legend.predictedDate: P-hat = your predicted next period start
legend.lutealLength: L = luteal phase length, in days
